claims.text: Conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing of AlCrFeNiSi powder produces high thermal gradients.
Conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing of AlCrFeNiSi powder produces significant residual stresses.
Conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing degrades the mechanical properties of AlCrFeNiSi components.
Conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing entails processing complexity for AlCrFeNiSi miniature components.
A machine-learning model can optimize laser pulse duration, power, and frequency to reduce cumulative thermal input during build-up.
Intermittent pulsed-laser energy input minimizes localized overheating.
Intermittent pulsed-laser energy input reduces thermal gradients.
Controlled pulsed energy deposition promotes a more uniform microstructure.
Controlled pulsed energy deposition produces fewer dislocations and residual-stress sites.
Replacing continuous high-energy deposition with lower-net-input pulsed deposition reduces peak temperatures in the material.
Reduced peak temperatures and thermal gradients minimize the development of residual stresses.
The pulsed regime refines the microstructure.
The ML-optimized pulsed regime will lower residual thermal stresses relative to conventional continuous high-thermal-load deposition.
The ML-optimized pulsed regime will increase yield strength relative to conventional continuous high-thermal-load deposition.
The ML-optimized pulsed regime will improve ductility relative to conventional continuous high-thermal-load deposition.
The ML-optimized pulsed regime will reduce the need for extensive post-processing and simplify the processing workflow.

The proposed processing window is AlCrFeNiSi powder, miniature component geometries, an inert-gas atmosphere, ambient starting conditions, matched build orientations, and comparable layer thicknesses.
The intervention may cease to be effective for larger geometries because scale effects can alter thermal dynamics.
